"Bosses 'increasingly reluctant' to hire as employment costs soar."

That was a Telegraph headline, with the Employment Rights Act's January deadline named right next to the costs. It's a story you'll keep hearing: give people rights at work and employers stop hiring.

So I went and looked at the figures.

Vacancies peaked at nearly 1.3 million in the spring of 2022. By October 2024, when the Employment Rights Bill was first put before Parliament, they were down to about 830,000. By the end of 2025, when the Act became law, they were down to about 740,000. The latest figure is 690,000.

So nearly all of the fall happened before the Act became law, and it started years before anyone had seen the Bill.

And most of the Act hasn't started yet. Sick pay from the first day off has. So has paternity leave from your first day in a job. Protection from unfair dismissal after six months, instead of two years, doesn't start until January. Guaranteed hours for people on zero-hours contracts don't even have a date.

The costs on employers are real. National Insurance, the minimum wage, energy, interest rates. Ministers are worried that some large employers, including banks, plan to use AI to cut staff. Rights at work are one thing on a long list.

In practice, if you're on low pay and too unwell to work, you now get sick pay from your first day off, instead of nothing for three days, or nothing at all. And from January, you won't have to be in a job for two years before you're protected from being let go without a fair reason. Money and job security are the worries people bring into training with them.

If a business only works while people can be let go without a fair reason for their first two years, the law isn't the problem.

Every QA Engineer Should Try Building at Least One AI Agent!

Here are 10 practical AI Agents that QA Engineers can build.

1. Requirement Review Agent
Reviews user stories and identifies missing acceptance criteria, edge cases, and unclear requirements.

2. Test Case Generation Agent
Generates positive, negative, boundary, and integration test scenarios from requirements.

3. API Contract Agent
Analyzes API specifications and suggests request validations, negative test cases, and schema checks.

4. Automation Code Review Agent
Reviews automation scripts and identifies hardcoded data, weak assertions, unstable locators, fixed waits, and duplicate code.

5. Failure Analysis Agent
Analyzes test reports, logs, and stack traces to classify failures as application defects, automation issues, test data problems, or environment failures.

6. Flaky Test Analysis Agent
Examines test execution history to identify frequently failing tests, failure patterns, and potential root causes.

7. Defect Drafting Agent
Converts logs, screenshots, and API responses into structured bug reports with clear reproduction steps.

8. Regression Test Selection Agent
Analyzes code changes, affected modules, and historical defects to recommend relevant regression test cases.

9. Test Execution Reporting Agent
Combines execution results, defect status, and testing progress into clear and concise QA reports.

10. Release Quality Analysis Agent
Analyzes test results, unresolved defects, and known risks to help QA teams prepare release-readiness reports.

You don't need to build 10 AI Agents. Start with one repetitive task, automate it, measure the results and improve it.

AI agents can now act for you. That is exactly why some tasks should stay human.

An agent that drafts a wrong email wastes a minute.

An agent that sends it to your whole customer list costs you trust.

The risk isn't that agents are dumb. It's that they can be confidently wrong, or tricked by hidden instructions in a web page or email (prompt injection).

So before handing anything over, I ask one question: if this goes wrong, can I undo it in five minutes?

If not, a human clicks the final button. That rules out:

→ Payments and money transfers
→ Signing contracts or accepting terms
→ Mass emails and bulk messages
→ Deleting data, or changing passwords, 2FA and recovery settings
→ Hiring decisions and public posts in your name

Even the makers agree. Anthropic says its new Claude Duet agent waits for approval before it sends, pays, signs or deletes anything.

What I'd happily hand over: research, first drafts, sorting an inbox, filling a cart and stopping before checkout.

The agent does the slow part. A human does the final click.

Which task would you never hand to an AI agent?

From 1 January 2027, the window to correct a hiring decision falls from two years to six months.

Under the Employment Rights Act 2025, the qualifying period for ordinary unfair dismissal claims in Great Britain drops to six months. Lawyers will cover contracts and policies. The bigger change for most businesses is on the hiring side.

If the window to correct a hiring decision is shorter, the quality of that decision matters more. The best protection is a better decision at the start:

1) Define what success looks like before the role is advertised
2) Use structured, evidenced assessment, including when AI is part of screening
3) Check the market before settling for a thin shortlist
4) Build onboarding check-points at months one, three and five
5) Take extra care with senior hires

If you're hiring in this space, a few things are worth doing now:
1. Test candidates on enterprise delivery, not just strategy & vision.
2. Pair research-led founders with product and CX leaders who have done this before, and make sure that pairing is explicit.
3. Move early. The leaders with this track record are in short supply, and they are talking to more than one company.

Most companies pick one AI model and send it everything. The support bot, the invoice parser, the meeting summarizer and the contract reviewer all hit the same frontier model at the same price.

It works. It's also like hiring a senior partner to sort the mail.

The fix is LLM model routing: send each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, and escalate only the hard ones.

The research is consistent:
- RouteLLM (Berkeley/LMSYS) cut costs by over 85% on MT Bench while keeping 95% of GPT-4's performance.
- FrugalGPT (Stanford) matched GPT-4 with up to 98% lower cost on its test tasks.
- AWS says Bedrock's prompt routing can cut costs by up to 30% without hurting accuracy.

But routing is a quality problem before it's a cost problem. Before you route anything:

1. Build an eval set from your own real requests.
2. Write down "good enough" per task type.
3. Score small, mid and frontier models on it.
4. Check results by segment, not just the average.
5. Log every routing decision so you can explain the bill.

Start with your highest-volume workload, a simple two-tier rule, and a fallback to your current model. Measure for a month.

Happy Friday, LinkedIn!

Jealous of all the awards nights? ✅
Jealous of all the Christmas party posts? ✅
Jealous of those with a job? ✅

I’m a social butterfly, and one of the hardest parts of being out of work is how lonely it gets. I miss being part of a team, having a reason to get stuck in on a Monday morning and having something to look forward to. Seeing everyone dressed up for awards nights and Christmas parties brings it home. I’d give anything to be part of a team again.

Someone asked me yesterday how the job search was going.

“A brick wall. A bloody big brick wall.”

That’s genuinely how it feels right now. People tell me it’s the market, and I know they mean well. I’ve said it to candidates myself. I understand now how little comfort it brings when you still need to find work.

I’m grateful to everyone who’s recommended me, tagged me in a role or put a word in for me. And after 22 years in recruitment, I’m genuinely at a loss as to why I still can’t get someone to hire me.

I have a good CV, great experience and very strong references. Surely this is a CEO, CPO or Hiring Manager that can see my worth and hire me. 😭 

Try hearing “no” day after day. Try coming off a call thinking it went well, being told you’ll hear something soon, then hearing absolutely nothing. 

And then there’s the endless stream of TA tasks. After 22 years of doing this job, being asked to prove I can do the basics, over and over again, can feel downright demeaning. It’s demoralising when you put the time in and still end up back where you started.

Do that enough times and you start questioning everything, including things you’ve spent years knowing you’re good at. It’s mentally draining.

And I know I’m bloody good at what I do.

• 22 years in TA and recruitment across internal TA, MSP, RPO, executive search and agency
• Global, hands-on delivery across tech, AI, software, hardware, semiconductors, sport, finance, banking, media and telecoms
• Open on title across TA Manager, TA Lead, Senior TA Partner, Client Services Manager and Recruitment Manager roles
• London-based and immediately available for permanent, contract, FTC or temporary work
• Series A, B and C experience building and scaling teams in fast-growing businesses, from hands-on hiring for niche roles to putting recruitment processes in place as headcount grows.

I need to find something quickly. Christmas is around the corner, and it’s hard to look forward to 2027 when I still don’t know what January looks like.

So if we’ve worked together, whether you were a colleague, someone I managed or a client, please think of me if you hear of something. If you know a hiring manager who could use an experienced recruiter who’ll roll their sleeves up from day one, I’d really appreciate you putting us in touch.

And to everyone who’s already tagged me, recommended me or sent a message to see how I’m doing, thank you. It makes this feel a little less lonely. 🎄 

RS

Economist Daniel Susskind was asked what will still be worth learning in ten years. His answer: literacy, maths and critical thinking. The basics are turning out to be the advanced skills.

Translated to business, that means reading a brief or a contract precisely, checking whether the numbers add up, and questioning a confident answer. With AI drafting summaries, forecasts and code, the job hasn't become smaller. It has moved to judging whether the output is right.

In the interview, he points to how maths teaching adapted to the calculator: one track using it, one without it, and both tested. He argues we need the same for AI.

That split is how we hire now.

Our engineers use AI every day, and it makes part of the work faster. But what a client pays for is the second track: spotting when the output is wrong, and doing the work when the tool can't.

Susskind also argues that the best answer to uncertainty is flexibility: retraining later in a career as seriously as at the start. For a consultancy, that isn't optional. Tech stacks and tooling change faster than any hiring plan.

69 applications. 20 first interviews. 1 signed contract.

That's the funnel Mads Lorentzen, a geophysicist, reports after his role was cut in late 2025. He ran the search with a framework he built on Claude Code, and he started as an AI engineer in June 2026.

He open-sourced it as AI Job Search. It's MIT licensed and has 73,000+ stars on GitHub.

The workflow is simple to describe:
1. /setup builds your profile from your CV, a LinkedIn export or an interview.
2. /scrape searches job boards and sorts postings by fit.
3. /apply evaluates the role, drafts a tailored CV and cover letter, has a second agent review them, then compiles the PDFs.

The drafter-reviewer split is the part I like. One agent writes, another critiques, and the output only ships after a revision pass.

The detail I'd copy is how he used it. He told every employer he was using AI, and he says it usually started a real technical conversation instead of counting against him.

Before you clone it, the README flags three things:
- Claude Code has no free tier, so you need a paid plan or API credits.
- Don't fork it for your own search. Forks of public repos are public, and your name, history and salary expectations end up in tracked files. Use a private copy.
- Job postings are treated as untrusted input, but those defences work at the instruction level and aren't a sandbox. Skim what was written before you hit send.

My take: AI won't fix a weak profile. It removes the Sunday of rewriting the same cover letter, so the time goes into picking better roles.

Headline: The Degree Is Dead. Long Live the Skill.
For decades, we were sold a specific promise: Finish university. Get the certificate. Secure your future.
That paper was a ticket. It said, “We watched this person for four years, and they didn’t break.” That was enough. Companies hired you based on that signal of endurance and compliance. You traded your labor for stability, and in return, you accepted a certain level of control.
But that paradigm is shattering.
The old contract—“I give you my time; you give me security”—is being rewritten by AI and automation. Companies are no longer just hiring bodies to fill seats; they are hiring outcomes.
Here is the new reality for every graduate entering the job market today:
The Certificate Is No Longer Enough.
A degree proves you can follow instructions. It doesn’t prove you can solve novel problems, adapt to rapid change, or wield new tools. In an age where AI can generate code, write copy, and analyze data faster than any human, the credential loses its premium.
Companies Are Not Going to Hire You Anymore (In the Old Sense).
They aren’t looking for someone to “stay for life.” They are looking for someone who can deliver value today. The era of lifelong employment is over. The era of portfolio careers has begun.
You Must Sell Your Ability, Not Your Potential.
Stop asking, “Can you hire me?”
Start asking, “What problem can I solve for you right now?”
The game has changed. The safety net is gone. But so is the ceiling.
If you want to survive this shift, stop treating your degree as a shield. Start treating it as a foundation. Build skills that AI cannot easily replicate: critical thinking, emotional intelligence, complex problem-solving, and the ability to connect dots across disciplines.
The certificate got you in the door. Your adaptability will keep you there.

Based on a true story. A very fresh one. (TL;DR at the end)
Today, a single phone call saved a client from a bad hire.

I'm consulting for a brand that's looking for someone to handle their online presence. A colleague shortlisted the owner of a "content agency" and simply asked him for a content calendar proposal, leaving the scope and the pricing completely up to him.

On that first call, he promised as many reels as the videographer could shoot, made it sound like he'd be on set (for an extra fee, of course), and quoted $250.

Then I took the screening call.

We never asked for his cheapest option. He opened with it anyway: his lowest package, 2 reels and 6 carousels for $200.
So I asked what the $250 he quoted my colleague included. 2 reels and 6 carousels.
Same deliverables. Different price. And "as many reels as possible" had become two.

So I asked a few more questions.
Do you manage the paid ads? No.
Will you appear in the reels? No.
Will you be on set for the shoots? No. He writes the scripts, and if he's needed on set, we cover his transportation.

What about the strategy? He'd build it "according to his research". 🧐

I asked why the same package had two prices. "It depends on the business."
Fair enough. So what do you know about this business?
He hadn't read the brand blueprint we'd shared. He said he doesn't work that way.

Then I mentioned two things: no AI visuals, and everything must follow the brand guidelines.
That's when the call went downhill.

I asked for his portfolio and the two sample scripts we had requested to see his thinking. He said he'd send them.

Shortly after we hung up, he messaged my colleague: too busy, can't proceed.
No portfolio. No scripts. No brief read.

And to be clear, I know $200 doesn't buy you a full marketing team. I wasn't expecting miracles from that package. The price was never the problem. The method was.

Because this is exactly how many small businesses get scammed on marketing. Not through one big fraud, but through promises that shrink after the first call, prices that change depending on who's asking, "strategies" based on nobody knows what, and "agencies" that disappear the moment someone asks for proof.

Most founders don't have time to ask those questions. And if you don't work in marketing, you don't know which ones to ask.

That's what a consultant is for. Not to make the content, but to make sure the person making it is worth the money:
→ defining what the business actually needs before anyone quotes a price
→ asking for proof of work, not promises
→ comparing offers on the same scope, so prices and promises can't move around
→ making sure everything follows the brand, not whatever is fastest to generate
→ spotting the red flags before the contract, not after the invoice

The cheapest option in this story was never going to be cheap. A $200 package with no strategy, no ads, no presence and no portfolio costs you the $200, plus the months you lose finding out.

Founders, what's the first question you ask before hiring someone for your content?

TL;DR: A "content agency" quoted two prices for the same package, promised more than he could deliver, skipped the brief, and disappeared when we asked for proof. 
The cheap option is rarely cheap. Ask questions before you sign.

When we automate something at Akveo, first we try to put each task on two axes: what the employee can do, and what AI can do. There is a framework like this, called SCAN, and it really helps to figure it out. Depending on the task, you land in one of four zones.

- Substitute. Employee can't, AI can. For example, someone who never wrote code asks AI to make an app, and it works. But this is risky, because if you don't understand it, you can't check it.

- Complement. Both can. Lawyer can write a contract, AI makes the first draft and the lawyer checks it.

- Aid. Nobody can do it alone. Employee knows a bit and AI helps with the rest, like when you can make a chart but never made a dashboard.

- Non-negotiable. Only the employee. Hiring, ethics, things where a person has to take responsibility.

Try it on your own tasks. We do, and it helps.

"AI experience" on a CV has stopped meaning much.

That is how one UK recruiter, Kieran Scully of Wave Talent, put it to ContractorUK this month, and the numbers behind it explain why. The REC's index of demand for temporary tech staff reached 53.7 in September, its highest since January 2023. Adzuna counted 25,000 UK job adverts mentioning AI in September, up from 14,700 a year earlier. The REC listed AI/ML developers and engineers as in short supply for both contract and permanent roles.

When demand jumps like that, every CV starts to say AI.

Scully says hiring managers now dig into evals, observability, guardrails and systems with real users. I think that is the right instinct. "Have you used AI tools?" tells you very little. These tell you more:

• What did you build, and who used it?
• How did you check the output was good enough?
• What did you watch once it was live?
• What stopped it doing something it shouldn't?
• What went wrong, and what did you change?

People who have shipped AI answer with specifics and a few scars. Weaker answers stay at the level of tool names.

At MedRec Technologies we build engineering teams in India, the UK and the USA, and I would use the same questions in all three.

Hiring managers: what is the one question that tells you someone has really shipped AI?

When a coding agent edits a Databricks Lakeflow pipeline directly, it often discovers errors only when Databricks plans the graph. It fixes one error, submits again, and discovers the next. Each loop can cost hours.

So we moved the model into formal, locally testable ODCS data contracts and built a small transpiler that turns them into native Lakeflow declarations. The agent edits the contract, validates the schema, dependency graph, joins, and expressions locally, then runs Spark fixtures to check the results. Databricks runs natively with all it's features.
Since the switch, every pipeline in this workflow has planned successfully.

Once again, in an AI native project, the guardrail is the most important engineering deliverable. It gives the agent a way to catch and fix errors before submitting a pipeline run.

Yesterday, we walked through this with the Databricks team at our vVARDIS HQ. We also discussed where the pattern could go next, including using those same contracts to feed our Databricks ontology. Once central clean abstraction.

Thank you to the Databricks team for visiting and working through this with us.

PS: any idea on how to do this in better way? we're hiring :)

I’m looking for a job DAY 61 

Don't count your chickens before they hatch 🐣
I learned this one the hard way on day 61 of my job search.

I turned down an offer in November, betting on another company. That bet didn't pay off 

For most of my life I was running after income, and I changed about 10 professions before I found marketing. Now, for the first time, I'm not looking for just a paycheck. I'm looking for a place where I can actually grow and build my career 🌱 Maybe that's why I took the risk

So here's what 61 days of job hunting actually taught me:

🧩 To stop losing track of 250+ applications, I built a tracker with AI that sends me a fresh vacancy digest every morning, with a match score for each role

🧩 To turn rejections into something useful, I started asking for feedback every single time. Most companies stay silent, but one gave me a full breakdown after a test task, and it changed how I prepare for every interview since

🧩 To survive the European job market, I had to adapt to a completely different pace. In Ukraine, hiring is much simpler: a couple of calls, a test task, and you can get an offer within a week or two. In European companies, the full cycle can take 3 to 6 months, with more stages, more people involved and a lot more waiting in between

🧩 To never repeat the November mistake, I now keep several processes going until a contract is actually signed

150+ rejections, 1 declined offer, and a few interviews still in progress. Not the story I planned, but definitely the one that taught me the most 🖤

A quick snapshot of some trends I've seen in the market this November across the UAE /GCC 📊
 
🔹 Investment keeps growing. Global tech vendors are expanding their regional offices and partner networks, which is creating a steady flow of new data projects.
 
🔹 AI is driving demand. Organisations are moving AI from pilots into production, and they're finding it only works with clean, well-governed data underneath.
 
🔹 Governance has gone mainstream. Data protection laws and national data strategies across the region are making cataloguing, lineage and data quality a priority at board level.
 
🔹 Hybrid skills win. The most sought-after engineers can build modern data platforms and understand governance, metadata and security. That combination is rare.
 
🔹 Contracts are booming. Consultancies and government programmes want senior contractors on 6–24 month engagements who can start immediately.
 
Candidates: pipeline skills alone won't get you shortlisted. Governance and AI-readiness experience is what makes you stand out.

Hiring managers: the talent pool is small and good people go within days, so move fast.

What’s happening? German enterprise software company SAP is preparing to #cut at least 10,000 #jobs as it transforms its software business for the AI era, according to people familiar with the matter. All departments have been asked to identify potential cuts, particularly in product, engineering, and sales teams.
SAP SE is preparing a major restructuring plan to eliminate at least 10,000 jobs, roughly 9% of its global workforce of over 110,000 employees, as it pivots to an #AI-first business model.
Reported by Bloomberg, the move is driven by CEO Christian Klein's push to fundamentally redesign how the Walldorf-based software giant develops, embeds AI into, and sells its enterprise applications.

#Affected #Teams. While every department has been asked to identify potential cost reductions, product development, engineering, and sales teams face the heaviest scrutiny.
#Executive Shakeups. The layoffs follow two executive board reorganizations in 2026. Two of SAP's six board members are set to depart in March 2027: product chief Muhammad Alam did not renew his contract (with Klein absorbing most of his duties), and sales chief Thomas Saueressig announced he is leaving to become #CEO of IONOS Group.
Negotiations & German Protections. The exact number of cuts is not yet finalized and depends on upcoming negotiations with employee representatives. In Germany, where SAP's largest employee base is located, the company's labor council recently secured an employment guarantee running through the end of 2028. This requires SAP to offer affected German staff alternative internal roles and retraining, meaning outright layoffs may disproportionately hit international markets.
Timeline. SAP has not officially confirmed the plans, stating only that it continuously reviews its organization. Historically, the company announces major restructuring initiatives alongside its full-year financial results in late #January.

#Second #Overhaul in Three Years. This would be SAP’s second major workforce reduction in under three years. In early 2024, SAP executed a €3 #billion restructuring that eliminated roughly 10,000 #roles. However, through voluntary buyouts, retraining, and aggressive hiring in AI and cloud sectors, SAP's overall headcount actually grew slightly through 2025 and 2026.
#Financial Paradox. The cuts are not driven by immediate financial distress. In Q3 2026, #SAP posted #record #quarterly #revenue exceeding €10 #billion (up 13% year-over-year) and saw cloud revenue jump 26%. Instead, the company is trimming legacy operations and restricting non-AI spending, following a July 2026 hiring and travel freeze, to fund #AI #acquisitions and #infrastructure.

It's been a funny old week 🌚 Do you believe the old wives' tale about the moon affecting our moods and energy? I'm half tempted to, because it explains a lot about "those" kinds of weeks.
 
Moon and madness aside, I've been dipping my toe back into sourcing and screening as part of my role here at Scede. I've been so impressed by the LinkedIn profiles I've come across and how well people sell themselves. Then there are a few that need a little work.
 
If you're in TA and want to be spotted, here's what makes a headhunter stop scrolling:

📍 Say where you're based, right at the top
 Your location, not your employer's head office. It's a great place to note your current role and industry too! e.g. "Embedded Talent Partner | SaaS and Fintech | Based in Belfast, open to remote"

🏢 Name your models and markets
 Agency, RPO or embedded? SaaS, Fintech or Gaming? Startup, scaleup or enterprise? These are the exact words we search for.

🎯 Show what you hire for and how
 List the roles you've filled, plus your sourcing tools and ATS: LinkedIn Recruiter, Juicebox, Greenhouse, Ashby.

🤖 Make your AI, automation and data skills visible
 More hiring teams are looking for them. AI assisted sourcing, automated scheduling, data metrics and funnel reporting all count.

🏆 Shout about your wins
 Numbers stand out.
 e.g. "28 hires in 12 months with 92% offer acceptance"

⏳ Give short roles/ tenure some context
 The last few years have been tough on TA, and short stints rarely tell the whole story. Adding "contract" or "role made redundant" reassures embedded clients that you'll stay the course.

It won't apply to everyone. But if you're thinking about taking a leap, a little profile admin tidy up could be the difference between being scrolled past and getting that message.

Who's hiring and cutting in Germany this week: Agon raises $70M, Ryanair offers 1k+ jobs if the aviation tax goes, Lufthansa cuts around 1k

I am doing weekly roundups of who's raising, expanding and cutting in Germany in Careers newsletter on Thursday. Here is a part of it:

**Just raised money **

- Agon (Berlin, defence AI and autonomous systems): $70M Series A
- Dcubed (Munich, satellite deployment and power systems): €27.2M Series A
- Playbook (Munich, rulebook layer for regulated-industry AI): €8M
- Vetaion (Munich, automated control cabinet factory): €5.7M pre-seed
- eventfirst (Berlin, AI platform for corporate events): €4.5M pre-seed
- Solistiq (Würzburg, AI inventory and demand planning): €2M pre-seed
- Paligo (Burkau, regional pallet goods marketplace): €1.5M
- AI-Z (Stuttgart, AI rollout with a data-leak firewall): undisclosed

**Expanding**

- Ryanair (Ireland, airline) promised $3.6B of investment in Germany, 250 new routes and more than 1k jobs by 2032, on condition that the aviation tax is abolished entirely and airport, air traffic control and security fees fall.
- N26 (Berlin, neobank) wants to at least double its customer count by 2030 and announced new products.
- PAIR Finance (Berlin, debt collection software) raised €100M in debt with its first bond and plans acquisitions and new markets. A new HarbourVest-led fund is taking over Pollen Street's stake, at a valuation above €500M.
- Celonis (Munich, software) won the North Rhine-Westphalia police contract to replace Palantir's data analysis software, for up to seven years.

**Cutting**

- Lufthansa (Cologne, airline) wants to cut around 1k jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs. When and how is unclear.
- Galeria (Essen, department stores) is closing three stores, in Berlin, Cologne and Munich. Reportedly only about half of its current stores will remain.
- Hellweg (Dortmund) and Baywa's Bau- & Gartenmärkte (DIY stores) have closed for good across Germany, with a small part continuing under other brands.
- The Platform Group (Düsseldorf, e-commerce) has two more subsidiaries in insolvency, Digitec Living Brands and the former Fashionette GmbH.
- Walberg Urban Electrics (Hamburg), the maker of Egret e-scooters, is insolvent.
- Games: Berlin's games industry employs an estimated 2.5-4k people (of 12k in Germany). Studios are cutting capacity and laying off staff.

**Office & pay**

- Volkswagen (Wolfsburg, autos) set its negotiation position: zero pay rises and cuts to the 35-hour week.
- IG Metall Küste is extending warning strikes in northern Germany's metal and electrical industry with another 24-hour strike, after workers across the country stopped work last Friday.

That was it, see you next week!

AI in industrial companies might be THE most exciting place to build right now. 🏭 💪 

Some of the world's best industrial companies are right on Europe's doorstep, and more and more of them are starting to let AI do real work in procurement, controlling and planning. Two of our portfolio companies are currently hiring for exactly that. 

But "starting" is the key word. In coding, AI has spread incredibly fast. In industrial back offices, almost everyone has tried a pilot, and far fewer have something running every day.

From what I see, that gap gets closed in a very hands-on way: someone sits with the customer for weeks, connects SAP and a handful of other systems and works through every exception. That's what Forward-Deployed Engineers do, and demand for them has exploded this year.

The catch: this doesn't scale. You can't hire one FDE per customer forever, and months of setup are where enthusiasm dies. So the teams I find most interesting turn every deployment into product, so the next customer sees value in days, not quarters.

Delvo makes sure the buyer is the best-prepared person in the room. It combines a company's own spend and contract data with market intelligence, so buyers walk into every supplier negotiation knowing exactly where their leverage is. BSH, OMV and ElringKlinger use it and have cut negotiation prep time by up to 90%. New customers go live within days, not after months of setup. Erik Oberländer, Jonas Keutel and Darius Dresp bring experience from 500+ supplier negotiations at PwC and from building AI products and ventures at McKinsey. They're hiring in Berlin across engineering, deployment and ops.

Zeit AI (YC S24) is basically the data engineer most companies wish they had, without the hiring. Connect ERP, CRM and the rest, ask a question in plain language, and get a dashboard or report back. Customers usually see first results on their own data within days, not after a six-month IT project. Siemens, AT&S and HORSCH are customers. Leopold von Waldthausen and Marvin Bornstein come from Palantir and have built a team with alumni from Yale, Oxford and HPI. They're growing fast in Munich across engineering, sales, growth and HR.

In both teams, you'd own real problems from day one and learn how large industrial companies work from the inside. If you'd like to be one of the people closing that gap, have a look at their open roles. Or just drop me a message and I'll happily make an intro.

After 25 years in corporate, I spent 18 months in Web3. It didn't work out.

(Most of those projects have since closed. What I learned from them hasn't.)

After leaving the corporate world, I wanted to explore what came next.

I was genuinely fascinated by the technology. How blockchain and smart contracts could change the way businesses work.

So I got stuck in.

→ Joined project communities and got to know the founders and what they were building
→ Advised two Web3 projects on roadmaps, pitch decks, and fundraising
→ Learned how to take an idea to a prototype and an MVP, with real feedback from the community

What surprised me was how naturally my corporate experience transferred.

Years of building business cases and convincing senior leadership to approve enterprise-wide projects turned out to be exactly what many early founders were missing.

But the space was too early.

Lots of big ideas. Not always the experience to deliver them.

So nothing landed. Quite a few of the people I met then have since moved into AI.

What I did come away with was two things 25 years in corporate hadn't given me:

1. The mindset to work without the structure I'd always had
2. The confidence to start my own business

That's how I'd explain those 18 months to a hiring manager today.

Not as a gap. As a chapter with a beginning, a middle, and an outcome.

If your career has taken a detour, do the same:

1. Name it: what you were doing, not "career break"
2. Show what you did: the projects, the skills, the people
3. Connect it: what it led to, and why that makes sense

Senior careers aren't always straight lines.

They only look like gaps when nobody explains them.

🚨 We're Hiring: Cybersecurity Talent for an AI Lab Project (100% Remote | Contract) 🚨
We're building a pod of cybersecurity professionals to support a leading AI lab. You'll help train and evaluate AI models on security topics. Three roles are open, from early-career to principal level.

🔹 Principal Cybersecurity Expert
Lead a full-time pod of about 10 experts. You'll set guidelines, make the final call on policy-sensitive cases, and be the main domain voice with the client.
✔️ 8–15 years of hands-on experience (SOC, IR, threat intel, AppSec, pentesting, vuln research)
✔️ Experience leading or mentoring analysts
✔️ Working experience with LLMs
✔️ Sound judgment on responsible disclosure and dual-use content
✔️ Preferred: OSCP, OSCE, GXPN, GCIH or CISSP


🔹 Senior Cybersecurity Expert
Handle the harder labeling and investigation cases, own QC for the pod, run calibration sessions, and guide Junior analysts.
✔️ 5–8 years in security operations, IR, threat hunting, AppSec, pentesting, malware analysis or cloud security
✔️ Experience using, testing or evaluating LLMs
✔️ Experience reviewing others' work or mentoring
✔️ Comfortable reading code (Python, C/C++, JS, Go)


🔹 Cybersecurity Expert (Analyst)
Label and investigate security data, check exploits and techniques, look up CVEs and MITRE ATT&CK, and write clear rationales.
✔️ Up to 5 years of experience, including internships, SOC, CTF or bug bounty work
✔️ Bachelor's or master's in cybersecurity, CS or a related field
✔️ Solid fundamentals in networking, OS, web security and OWASP Top 10
✔️ Python skills and familiarity with Burp Suite, Wireshark, Nmap, Ghidra or a SIEM

📌 Good to know
Remote, contract-based
Full-time availability required, with no competing full-time commitments
Engagements run 6–12 months (Principal and Senior roles)


📩 How to apply: Send your CV to hr@herleads.com with the role you're applying for in the subject line.
Know someone who'd be a great fit? Tag them or share this post. Referral bonuses apply! 🤝
